message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"2.5","text":"Peter, greatly pleased at this, answered, “Your being set right has now reached completion, now that you have recognized the greatness of unerring prophecy, without which it is impossible for anyone to obtain what is supremely beneficial. For although many and diverse good things exist among the things that are or can come to be, the most blessed of all—whether it is eternal life, lasting health, perfect intellect, light, joy, incorruptibility, or any other thing that exists or can exist as a surpassing good in the nature of beings—cannot be acquired in any other way unless one first knows the things that exist as they are. And that knowledge cannot be attained in any other way unless one first recognizes the prophet of truth.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἡ πρὸς σὲ διόρθωσις","chosen":"your being set right","rationale":"διόρθωσις can mean correction, reform, or rectification; the passive English wording makes Peter’s addressee the person corrected without implying that he performs the correction."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ἀπταίστου προφητείας","chosen":"of unerring prophecy","rationale":"ἀπταίστος denotes freedom from stumbling or error; “unerring” preserves the epistemic emphasis, though “infallible prophetic revelation” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἐν ὑπεροχῇ συμφέρον","chosen":"what is supremely beneficial","rationale":"The phrase denotes the beneficial thing that stands preeminent, rather than merely something advantageous."},{"source_quote":"παράμονος ὑγεία","chosen":"lasting health","rationale":"παράμονος describes something enduring or abiding; “lasting” avoids suggesting that ordinary health is necessarily permanent."},{"source_quote":"τὰ ὄντα ὡς ἔστιν","chosen":"the things that exist as they are","rationale":"This preserves the ontological wording of τὰ ὄντα and the claim that they must be known according to their actual state."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἡ πρὸς σὲ διόρθωσις τέλος εἴληφεν, ἐπεγνωκότα","issue":"The accusative participle ἐπεγνωκότα has no explicit accusative head following the nominative clause. It can defensibly be understood by sense as referring back to σὲ, hence “now that you have recognized”; the construction is anacoluthic but intelligible, so the printed wording is retained.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"2.6","text":"A prophet of truth is one who always knows all things: things past as they happened, things occurring as they occur, and things to come as they will be; he is free from error, merciful, and the only one entrusted to set forth the truth. Read, and you will find those who thought they could discover the truth by themselves....... For this is distinctive of a prophet: to disclose the truth, just as it is distinctive of the sun to bring the day. For this reason, all who ever desired to know the truth but were not fortunate enough to learn it from him came to the end of their lives still seeking and without finding. For how could someone who seeks the truth obtain it from his own ignorance? Even if he finds it, because he does not know it, he passes it by as though it did not exist. Nor, for that matter, will he be able to grasp truth from someone else (someone who likewise, out of ignorance, claims to possess knowledge), except only with respect to conduct—and even then only that conduct which can be recognized because it is reasonable, and which, from each person’s not wishing to be wronged, presents to him the knowledge that he must not wrong another.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀναμάρτητος","chosen":"free from error","rationale":"The adjective can mean “sinless” or “infallible”; the surrounding description of comprehensive knowledge and truthful instruction favors freedom from error."},{"source_quote":"μόνος τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑφηγεῖσθαι πεπιστευμένος","chosen":"the only one entrusted to set forth the truth","rationale":"ὑφηγεῖσθαι can mean to guide, explain, or set forth, while πεπιστευμένος presents the prophet as uniquely entrusted with this task."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ὁμοίως ἐξ ἀγνωσίας γνῶσιν ἔχειν ἐπαγγελλομένου","chosen":"someone who likewise, out of ignorance, claims to possess knowledge","rationale":"ἐξ ἀγνωσίας is taken with the act of claiming, emphasizing the claimant’s ignorance; it could alternatively be heard as the paradoxical “claims to possess knowledge derived from ignorance.”"},{"source_quote":"πλὴν πολιτείας μόνης","chosen":"except only with respect to conduct","rationale":"πολιτεία may denote conduct, a way of life, or civic order. The following rule against wronging another shows that moral conduct is intended; “with respect to” makes the scope of the attainable truth explicit."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸ εὔλογον γνωρισθῆναι δυναμένης","chosen":"which can be recognized because it is reasonable","rationale":"τὸ εὔλογον denotes the rule’s reasonable or rationally evident character, not prophetic disclosure."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":".......","issue":"The printed sequence of seven periods marks an explicit gap after νομίσαντας. The supplied Greek contains no text with which to restore the omitted material, so the gap is preserved without conjecture.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"2.7","text":"All, then, who ever sought what is true, trusting themselves to be able to find it, were ensnared. This is precisely what the Greek philosophers and the more earnest among the barbarians have suffered. For, drawing on conjectures as they applied themselves to visible things, they pronounced on things unseen, supposing that whatever happened in any way to present itself to them was true. For, as though they knew the truth, those who are still seeking the truth reject some of the notions that present themselves to them and confirm others, as though they knew, although they do not know which are true and which are false. And those searching for truth lay down doctrines about truth, not knowing that one who seeks truth cannot learn it from his own error. For, as I said, he cannot even recognize it when it is present, since it is the very thing he does not know.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐνηδρεύθησαν","chosen":"were ensnared","rationale":"The passive verb evokes being caught by an ambush or trap; “ensnared” preserves that image."},{"source_quote":"ἐκ στοχασμῶν γὰρ ἐπιβάλλοντες τοῖς ὁρατοῖς","chosen":"drawing on conjectures as they applied themselves to visible things","rationale":"ἐπιβάλλειν with the dative can describe directing or applying oneself to something. “Drawing on conjectures” preserves ἐκ στοχασμῶν without claiming that the visible things themselves are conjectural."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ὁπώσποτε παραστὰν αὐτοῖς","chosen":"whatever happened in any way to present itself to them","rationale":"ὁπώσποτε stresses the indeterminate manner in which a notion occurs, while παραστάν depicts it as presenting itself."},{"source_quote":"ὑπολήψεων ἃ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζουσιν, ἃ δὲ κρατύνουσιν","chosen":"notions that present themselves to them ... reject some ... and confirm others","rationale":"ὑπόληψις here denotes a conception or supposition, and κρατύνειν means to strengthen, establish, or confirm it."},{"source_quote":"δογματίζουσιν περὶ ἀληθείας","chosen":"lay down doctrines about truth","rationale":"δογματίζειν means to formulate or assert authoritative opinions; “lay down doctrines” preserves its force without importing a later ecclesiastical sense."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.8","text":"But what persuades each person who seeks to learn from himself is not invariably what is true, but what is pleasing. Since, then, one thing pleases one person and another thing another, a different thing holds sway over each as true. But what is true is what the prophet holds to be true, not what is pleasant to each person. For the one would be many if what is pleasing were true, which is impossible. This is also why the word-lovers among the Greeks (not wisdom-lovers), having approached matters through conjectures, laid down many different doctrines. They supposed that the internal coherence of their hypotheses was truth, not knowing that, once they had defined false starting points for themselves, their conclusion had indeed come into agreement with their starting point.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἄλλου ἄλλο κρατεῖ ὡς ἀληθές","chosen":"a different thing holds sway over each as true","rationale":"κρατεῖ with the genitive portrays each person as governed by a different purported truth; alternatives include “each holds a different thing as true.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ δοκοῦν τῷ προφήτῃ","chosen":"what the prophet holds to be true","rationale":"δοκεῖν may mean “seem,” “appear good,” or “judge.” The contrast with each person’s pleasure favors the prophet’s judgment, while the supplied “to be true” is the contextual complement."},{"source_quote":"πολλὰ γὰρ ἂν ἦν τὸ ἕν","chosen":"the one would be many","rationale":"The deliberately abstract contrast between the one and the many is retained; context identifies “the one” with truth, but the Greek does not repeat the noun."},{"source_quote":"οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων φιλόλογοι (οὐ φιλόσοφοι)","chosen":"the word-lovers among the Greeks (not wisdom-lovers)","rationale":"The etymological rendering preserves the author’s contrast between φιλόλογοι and φιλόσοφοι; the neutral modern term “philologists” would obscure the wordplay."},{"source_quote":"τὴν οἰκείαν τῶν ὑποθέσεων ἀκολουθίαν","chosen":"the internal coherence of their hypotheses","rationale":"ἀκολουθία denotes logical sequence or consistency, while οἰκεία marks it as belonging intrinsically to the hypotheses; “proper sequence” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ψευδεῖς ἀρχὰς ἑαυτοῖς ὁρισαμένων, τῇ μὲν ἀρχῇ αὐτῶν τὸ τέλος συμφωνίαν εἴληφεν","chosen":"once they had defined false starting points for themselves, their conclusion had indeed come into agreement with their starting point","rationale":"ἀρχή and τέλος are rendered as logical starting point and conclusion, preserving the claim that consistency with false premises does not establish truth."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
